===
皇上節儉之性成於
天縱易簡之德懋於日新日與二三大臣前籌
而講畫者莫非爲天下愛惜此財計是故
一
賞賚也必宗伯曰可左右大臣曰可然後給
之而禮無闕施矣一興作也必司空曰可
左右大臣曰可然後舉之而工無闕費矣
一經用也必司農曰可左右大臣曰可然
後取之而
punctuated: 以同符二祖，重光列聖，而陋漢文於不居矣。薄海內外，罔不舉手加額而歌皇仁，誠千萬禩一時也。即有司者，何敢以不肖之心應之，而不思所以仰承德意乎？第經費有常，歲出不可省；而詔免積逋，歲入不及額。其所以濟盈縮以裕公私之用者，果安在哉？蓋我皇上節儉之性成於天縱，易簡之德懋於日新，日與二三大臣前籌而講畫者，莫非爲天下愛惜此財計。是故一賞賚也，必宗伯曰可，左右大臣曰可，然後給之，而禮無闕施矣；一興作也，必司空曰可，左右大臣曰可，然後舉之，而工無闕費矣；一經用也，必司農曰可，左右大臣曰可，然後取之，而
translation_en: …whereby it matches the tallies of the Two Ancestors (Taizu and Taizong), adds luster to the succession of Imperial Sages, and disdains Emperor Wen of Han as unworthy of comparison. Within and beyond the seas, there is no one who does not raise their hands to their foreheads in celebration and sing the praises of Imperial benevolence; truly, this is a moment that comes once in ten thousand generations. Even as for the authorities, how could they dare respond with unworthy hearts and fail to ponder how to reverently carry out His virtuous intentions? Yet regular expenditures are fixed, and annual outlays cannot be reduced; whereas the imperial decree remits accumulated arrears, so annual revenues fall short of the quota. Wherein, then, lies the means to balance surpluses and deficits so as to enrich both public and private needs? It is because our August Emperor's frugal nature is perfected by Heaven-bestowed genius, and His virtue of ease and simplicity flourishes through daily renewal. What He deliberates and plans each day with two or three Grand Ministers is nothing other than cherishing and sparing these financial resources for the sake of the realm. Therefore, whenever there is a bestowal of rewards, the Minister of Rites (zongbo) must say it is permissible, and the Grand Ministers of the Left and Right must say it is permissible, before it is granted—and thus ritual lacks no proper dispensation. Whenever there is a construction project, the Minister of Works (sikong) must say it is permissible, and the Grand Ministers of the Left and Right must say it is permissible, before it is undertaken—and thus public works suffer no wasteful expense. Whenever there is a regular expenditure, the Minister of Revenue (sinong) must say it is permissible, and the Grand Ministers of the Left and Right must say it is permissible, before it is drawn—and thus…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
上供無闕需矣語云
朝廷之一金民間之百金也
朝廷之百金民間之萬金也
皇上惜一金之費則天下饗百金之利惜百金
之費則天下饗萬金之利此便計之在民
間者也天下視以爲百金唯惜一金之費
而答其望天下視以爲萬金唯惜百金之
費而答其望此便計之在
朝廷者也以是
===
天恩浩蕩無病於民亦無病於
國信自有所本矣然非愚生之臆說也竊聞
皇上萬幾之暇
御書十二事扁之
內庭曰謹天戒曰任賢能曰親儒臣曰遠嬖
倖曰明賞罰曰審出入曰慎起居曰節飲
食曰收放心曰存敬畏曰納忠言所以備
觀省者亦既悉矣而歸於樽節用之一言
則
punctuated: 上供無闕需矣。語云：「朝廷之一金，民間之百金也；朝廷之百金，民間之萬金也。」皇上惜一金之費，則天下饗百金之利；惜百金之費，則天下饗萬金之利：此便計之在民間者也。天下視以爲百金，唯惜一金之費而答其望；天下視以爲萬金，唯惜百金之費而答其望：此便計之在朝廷者也。以是天恩浩蕩，無病於民，亦無病於國，信自有所本矣。然非愚生之臆說也。竊聞皇上萬幾之暇，御書十二事扁之內庭：曰謹天戒，曰任賢能，曰親儒臣，曰遠嬖倖，曰明賞罰，曰審出入，曰慎起居，曰節飲食，曰收放心，曰存敬畏，曰納忠言，所以備觀省者亦既悉矣，而歸於樽節用之一言，則
translation_en: … imperial supplies will suffer no deficiency in meeting what is required. As the saying goes: "One piece of gold at the imperial court is worth a hundred pieces of gold among the people; a hundred pieces of gold at the imperial court are worth ten thousand pieces of gold among the people." When His Majesty spares the expenditure of one piece of gold, the empire enjoys the benefit of a hundred pieces of gold; when He spares the expenditure of a hundred pieces of gold, the empire enjoys the benefit of ten thousand pieces of gold—this is the advantageous calculation that lies among the people. What the empire regards as a hundred pieces of gold requires only sparing the expenditure of one piece of gold to answer its hopes; what the empire regards as ten thousand pieces of gold requires only sparing the expenditure of a hundred pieces of gold to answer its hopes—this is the advantageous calculation that lies with the imperial court. Thus, that imperial grace flows vast and boundless, causing no harm to the people and likewise no harm to the state, truly has its foundation in this. Yet this is not the mere conjecture of this foolish student. I have humbly heard that in His leisure from the myriad affairs of state, His Majesty wrote out in His own hand twelve maxims and hung them on plaques in the inner palace: namely, "Heed the warnings of Heaven," "Employ the worthy and capable," "Draw close to Confucian ministers," "Keep favorites and sycophants at a distance," "Make rewards and punishments clear," "Scrutinize revenues and expenditures," "Be cautious in daily deportment," "Be moderate in food and drink," "Gather in the straying mind," "Preserve reverence and awe," and "Accept loyal remonstrance." That by which He provides for contemplation and self-examination is already exhaustive indeed, and yet it all comes down to the single phrase: "practice restraint and economize in expenditure." Thus…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
皇上之約已裕民非海內臣民所共覩記者乎
抑愚猶有獻焉夫節儉者人主之所難持
而羣變之所易奪者也出而接賢士大夫
知所謹也入而處燕閒隱僻則忽之矣出
而對圖書編簡以爲益也入而見紛華靡
麗則忘之矣故令德之主不惟其始而惟
其終昔曾肇欲以景德皇祐治平戶口墾
田較其入稽其費而得浮約爲省併計先
大學士丘濬亦欲以洪武永樂宣德正統
===
戶口墾田據其入考其出而得其盈虛之
數令心計臣䓂集以備
九重觀覽而堅定撙節愛養之心我
皇上節儉性成固無待於是者而臣子芹曝之
忱庶幾爲儉德永助云
第二問
張泰徵
同考試官教諭唐　批　論錢法洞悉本源而準諸理道
子其非言利士乎取之
punctuated:
皇上之約已裕民，非海內臣民所共覩記者乎？抑愚猶有獻焉：夫節儉者，人主之所難持，而羣變之所易奪者也。出而接賢士大夫，知所謹也；入而處燕閒隱僻，則忽之矣。出而對圖書編簡，以爲益也；入而見紛華靡麗，則忘之矣。故令德之主，不惟其始，而惟其終。昔曾肇欲以景德、皇祐、治平戶口墾田，較其入，稽其費，而得浮約，爲省併計；先大學士丘濬亦欲以洪武、永樂、宣德、正統戶口墾田，據其入，考其出，而得其盈虛之數，令心計臣䓂集，以備九重觀覽，而堅定撙節愛養之心。我皇上節儉性成，固無待於是者，而臣子芹曝之忱，庶幾爲儉德永助云。

第二問
張泰徵
同考試官教諭唐　批〔論錢法洞悉本源，而準諸理道。子其非言利士乎！取之。〕
translation_en:
… is His Majesty's restraining of himself to enrich the people not something that all officials and commoners within the seas have witnessed and remembered together? Yet this foolish student still has something to offer: frugality is something difficult for a ruler to maintain and easily snatched away by a multitude of distractions. When he goes out to meet worthy officials and grandees, he knows how to be cautious; when he retires to dwell in secluded leisure and private quarters, he neglects it. When he goes out to face books, charts, and bamboo slips, he regards them as beneficial; when he retires and sees dazzling luxury and extravagance, he forgets it. Therefore, a ruler of fine virtue does not merely attend to the beginning, but attends to the end. In the past, Zeng Zhao 曾肇 wished to take the figures for households, population, and reclaimed land from the Jingde (1004–1007), Huangyou (1049–1054), and Zhiping (1064–1067) eras, compare their revenues, audit their expenditures, and ascertain the surpluses and deficits in order to plan for reductions and consolidations. The former Grand Secretary Qiu Jun 丘濬 likewise wished to take the figures for households, population, and reclaimed land from the Hongwu (1368–1398), Yongle (1403–1424), Xuande (1426–1435), and Zhengtong (1436–1449) eras, rely on their revenues, examine their expenditures, and ascertain the numbers of their surpluses and deficits, having ministers skilled in fiscal calculation compile [?] them to provide for His Majesty's inspection in the Ninefold Palace and to firmly establish a mind of restraint and loving nourishment. Our Emperor is frugal by nature and surely has no need to depend on this, yet the humble sincerity of a subject offering wild celery and sunlight may perhaps serve as a lasting aid to his frugal virtue.

Second Question
Zhang Taizheng 張泰徵
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Tang 唐: [His discussion of monetary policy thoroughly understands the fundamental origins and measures them against principle and the Way. Is this gentleman not a scholar who refuses to speak of mere profit! Selected.]

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正梅　批〔條畫詳明有禆時務〕
考試官教授朱　批〔是攻古文辭者〕
治天下者利人者也非利於人者也夫治
以爲民利則其法必時所甚便而其制畫
必甚周卽卒然行之天下或泯泯失其依
違而上與下不異嚮頤指臂運若轉環然
私之蓄亦公之蓄是謂役財而卒未嘗不
國利也故利民之主也法治之幹也時事
之符也時以脩利利以度法法以建事而
===
治備矣嘗聞之昔人有言天下壤壤皆爲
利往故繩約之使不越均節之使各爭趨
在上耳自農工商交易之路通而錢幣興
焉聖王思以貿遷有無化居蓋自高辛時
業已創著陶唐氏謂之泉而虞因之夏后
氏謂之布而殷因之故伯禹鑄歷山之金
成湯鑄莊山之銅上古所造要適世用顧
法靡傳於紀籍莫得而攷云訖於成周制
乃大備太公望以尚父佐文武集大統立
punctuated:
考試官學正梅批〔條畫詳明，有禆時務。〕
考試官教授朱批〔是攻古文辭者。〕

治天下者，利人者也，非利於人者也。夫治以爲民利，則其法必時所甚便，而其制畫必甚周。卽卒然行之，天下或泯泯失其依違，而上與下不異嚮，頤指臂運，若轉環然。私之蓄亦公之蓄，是謂役財，而卒未嘗不國利也。故利，民之主也；法，治之幹也；時，事之符也。時以脩利，利以度法，法以建事，而治備矣。嘗聞之昔人有言：「天下壤壤，皆爲利往。」故繩約之使不越，均節之使各爭趨，在上耳。自農工商交易之路通，而錢幣興焉。聖王思以貿遷有無化居，蓋自高辛時業已創著。陶唐氏謂之泉，而虞因之；夏后氏謂之布，而殷因之。故伯禹鑄歷山之金，成湯鑄莊山之銅，上古所造，要適世用，顧法靡傳於紀籍，莫得而攷云。訖於成周，制乃大備。太公望以尚父佐文武集大統，立
translation_en:
Examiner Mei, Subprefectural Instructor (xuezheng), comments: [The analysis and planning are detailed and clear, beneficial to current affairs.]
Examiner Zhu, Prefectural Instructor (jiaoshou), comments: [This is one who has mastered ancient prose style.]

Those who govern the world bring benefit to others; they do not extract benefit from others. Now, when governance is aimed at benefiting the people, its laws will surely be most convenient for the times, and its institutional planning will surely be most comprehensive. Even if suddenly put into practice, so that the world in its confusion loses its usual hesitations, superiors and inferiors will not differ in their direction; directed by a nod of the chin and moved like an arm, it will operate like a turning ring. Private reserves are also public reserves: this is called putting wealth into service, and in the end it never fails to benefit the state. Therefore, benefit is the master of the people; law is the trunk of governance; timeliness is the tally of affairs. One uses timeliness to cultivate benefit, benefit to measure the law, and the law to establish affairs, and thus governance is complete. I have heard the saying of the ancients: "The whole world, in its bustling crowds, moves for the sake of profit." Therefore, restraining and binding them so that they do not overstep, and equalizing and regulating them so that each eagerly hastens forward, rests solely with those above. Ever since the paths of exchange among farmers, artisans, and merchants were opened, coined money has arisen. The sage kings sought to trade what one had for what one lacked and to circulate滯 goods; indeed, since the time of Gaoxin this had already been initiated and made manifest. The Taotang clan (Yao) called it "spring" (quan), and Yu (Shun) followed this; the Xiahou clan called it "cloth" (bu), and Yin (Shang) followed this. Thus, Earl Yu cast metal from Mount Li, and Tang the Completer cast copper from Mount Zhuang. What was created in high antiquity was in essence suited to the needs of the age, yet the methods were not transmitted in historical records, so there is no way to examine them. Down to the era of Completed Zhou, the system finally became fully developed. Taigong Wang, as Father-Advisor (Shangfu), assisted Kings Wen and Wu in consolidating the great succession; he established…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
圜法以通貨賄謂之九府大率毋子相權
互出以息而龜貝金錢刀布之流各得從
所宜爲幣尚故更調量之取勿滯也公旦
作周官立司市以政令禁物靡而均市以
商賈阜貨而行布以泉府同貨而斂賒若
泉府則掌征布於市斂貨之不售及滯於
民者以待不時之買或從民貸則辨授之
而定國服之息蓋微有所括於山澤工躔
之間而權其盈縮常在我然非利之也國
===
有凶荒始無征而作布未聞所謂私鑄令
也當是時天子治畿甸諸侯五服星列王
朝卿大夫各食邑不領於大府之經費邊
徼無戎馬調遣之煩徹法委輸特以供宗
廟朝聘乘輿御府等費而已入以制出出
必規入所謂錢幣者誠令上下僉饒足無
所窒格固非富强術也然其制僅一再見
於圜府周官而諸載記所睹寥寥焉至景
王始脩六錢之令是未必經久也說者謂
punctuated: 圜法以通貨賄，謂之「九府」。大率毋子相權，互出以息，而龜、貝、金、錢、刀、布之流，各得從所宜爲幣，尚故更調量之，取勿滯也。公旦作《周官》，立司市，以政令禁物靡而均市，以商賈阜貨而行布，以泉府同貨而斂賒。若泉府，則掌征布於市，斂貨之不售及滯於民者，以待不時之買；或從民貸，則辨授之，而定國服之息。蓋微有所括於山澤工躔之間，而權其盈縮常在我，然非利之也。國有凶荒，始無征而作布，未聞所謂私鑄令也。當是時，天子治畿甸，諸侯五服星列，王朝卿大夫各食邑，不領於大府之經費，邊徼無戎馬調遣之煩，徹法委輸，特以供宗廟、朝聘、乘輿、御府等費而已。入以制出，出必規入。所謂錢幣者，誠令上下僉饒足，無所窒格，固非富强術也。然其制僅一再見於圜府、《周官》，而諸載記所睹寥寥焉。至景王始脩大錢之令，是未必經久也。說者謂
translation_en: … the "Round Currency System" (Huanfa) to circulate goods and wealth, calling it the "Nine Repositories" (Jiufu). In general, heavy and light denominations ("mother and child") balanced one another, being issued alternately for relief and increase, while items such as tortoise shells, cowries, gold, coins, knife-money, and spade-money were each allowed to serve as currency according to what was suitable. They valued keeping to established usage while adjusting and measuring the supply, aiming solely to prevent stagnation. Duke Dan [the Duke of Zhou] composed the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), establishing the Director of Markets (Sishi) to prohibit extravagant goods and equalize market prices through administrative decrees, to enrich the supply of goods and circulate cloth-money through merchants, and to pool goods and manage collection and credit through the Monetary Directorate (Quanfu). As for the Monetary Directorate, it had charge of levying market-cloth in the marketplace and buying up goods that went unsold or stagnated among the people, holding them in readiness for unseasonable purchases; or, when the people sought loans, it distinguished and issued them while fixing interest rates proportional to state service obligations. Thus, while there was some slight extraction from mountains, marshes, artisans, and market stalls, and the power to balance surplus and scarcity always remained with the state, this was not done for profit. Only when the state suffered famine and dearth did it remit levies and mint coins; one never heard of any so-called decrees against private minting. At that time, the Son of Heaven governed the royal domain, the feudal lords were arrayed like stars across the Five Zones, and the Ministers and Grand Masters of the royal court each drew income from their own fiefs without being supported by the regular expenditures of the Grand Treasury (Dafu). The frontier marches were free from the trouble of mobilizing warhorses and troops, and the tax revenues conveyed under the tithing system (chefa) served merely to supply the expenses of the ancestral temples, court audiences and diplomatic missions, the imperial carriages, and the imperial household treasury. Expenditures were regulated according to revenues, and every expenditure was planned with revenue in mind. What was called currency truly served to make both superiors and inferiors abundant and self-sufficient without obstruction; it was decidedly not a technique for enriching the state and strengthening the military. Yet this system appears only once or twice in the Round Currency accounts and the Offices of Zhou, while references to it across other historical records are sparse indeed. By the time of King Jing [of Zhou], the decree for minting large coins (daqian, transcribed as liuqian 六錢 [?]) was first instituted, which shows that the earlier system did not necessarily endure for long. Commentators say that…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
周禮成書未及行殆其然矣漢承秦弊民
無藏蓋作業劇而財匱於是更鑄莢錢文
帝易之謂之四銖大較縱民得自鑄與時
休息而吳鄧錢遍天下姦盜益衆故私鑄
之禁生取懲不法一令也武帝置三官立
平準變赤側爲五銖而令郡國無鑄唐設
府院宋設諸路其稱名紛然未易指數大
抵百姓患苦其重艱於折易則引而之輕
流於符葉縱繰然應手輒破其弊至不可
===
數轉顧仍重之而當千當百蓋皆時其低
昂之柄而因以法乘除之俾可利國也惟
國之利而漫無當於羣庶之腴瘠非所爲
訓也然當是時漢唐人主雖稱利乃其全
盛天下類家給人足京師錢累巨萬貫朽
不可校斗米十錢公私浮物而桑旲之徒
始得以其心計幹畫而制其便彼緡筭榷
酤多不入好用之式爭獻少府以佐軍興
營建禱祀諸需而已雖損之下或益之上
punctuated: 《周禮》成書未及行，殆其然矣。漢承秦弊，民無藏蓋，作業劇而財匱，於是更鑄莢錢。文帝易之，謂之四銖，大較縱民得自鑄，與時休息，而吳鄧錢遍天下，姦盜益衆，故私鑄之禁生，取懲不法、一令也。武帝置三官，立平準，變赤側爲五銖，而令郡國無鑄。唐設府院，宋設諸路，其稱名紛然，未易指數。大抵百姓患苦其重，艱於折易，則引而之輕，流於符葉、縱繰，然應手輒破，其弊至不可數；轉顧仍重之，而當千、當百。蓋皆時其低昂之柄，而因以法乘除之，俾可利國也。惟國之利，而漫無當於羣庶之腴瘠，非所爲訓也。然當是時，漢唐人主雖稱利，乃其全盛，天下類家給人足，京師錢累巨萬，貫朽不可校，斗米十錢，公私浮物，而桑、旲之徒始得以其心計幹畫而制其便。彼緡筭、榷酤，多不入好用之式，爭獻少府，以佐軍興、營建、禱祀諸需而已。雖損之下，或益之上，
translation_en: … the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) was completed as a book before it could be put into practice—that is likely the case. When the Han inherited the exhaustion left by the Qin, the common people had neither savings nor roofs over their heads; labor was harsh and wealth was scarce, so they instead cast elm-pod coins (jiaqian). Emperor Wen changed them into what were called four-zhu coins. Broadly speaking, he allowed the people to cast coins themselves so as to give the age rest and recovery; yet the coins of the King of Wu and Deng Tong spread throughout the empire, and traitorous counterfeiters grew ever more numerous. Thus the prohibition against private casting arose, aimed at punishing lawlessness and unifying decrees. Emperor Wu established the Three Offices of the Shanglin Park, instituted the Bureau of Equalization and Standards (pingzhun), changed red-rimmed coins (chice) into five-zhu coins, and ordered that the commanderies and kingdoms cease casting. The Tang established directorates and courts, and the Song established coinages across the various circuits; their designations were so varied that they cannot easily be counted on the fingers. In general, when the common people suffered from coins being too heavy and difficult to convert and exchange, the state drew them toward lightness, degenerating into "talisman-leaf" (fuye) and "unreeled-silk" (zongshao) coins; yet these broke apart at the touch of the hand, and their abuses became too numerous to count. Turning back around, they again made them heavy, issuing coins worth a thousand or worth a hundred. All of this was a matter of timing the lever of raising and lowering values, using legal regulations to multiply and divide them so as to profit the state. Seeking only the profit of the state while paying no heed to the prosperity or destitution of the multitudes is no model to be taught. Yet at those times, although the rulers of Han and Tang spoke of profit, in their heyday the empire was generally well-supplied in every household and self-sufficient in every person: in the capital, cash accumulated by the tens of millions until the strings rotted and could no longer be tallied; a peck of grain cost ten cash; public and private goods overflowed; and only then were men like Sang Hongyang and Diwu Qi able to use their mental calculations and administrative schemes to engineer their own advantage. Those taxes on strings of cash (minsuan) and monopolies on liquor (quegu) mostly did not enter into the regular formulas for sound currency, as officials vied to present revenues to the Lesser Treasury (Shaofu) merely to assist with military mobilizations, construction projects, prayers, and sacrifices. Even though it diminished those below, it at least benefited those above; …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
彼其錢之弊固止輕重銖兩之間而非甚
有所壅閼也夫輕重數易則下擾故惟五
銖開元最中焉而開元迄今且傳之謂通
塞不關於是不其然矣故錢幣在周利人
者也漢以後利國者也乃
今日視周漢則又有大不然者內而
宗廟聘享乘輿御府外而
宗藩百官邊鄙將士有一弗藉於民者乎正
自總秷米粟藁絲餘自關梁市肆鹽鐵有
===
一弗藉於官者乎賦盡無益地而泉府斂
布之法難究詰矣利盡無逸貨而榷酤市
占之法旣舉矣未豐其流先恐竭其源噫
此所謂時也聖人不必於時能必時之不
違則制而通之以法法者所以因時布利
庇民者也若曰時不可而并法廢焉不亦
以噎忘餐乎我
國家自
太祖開天建極創通寶者二
punctuated: 彼其錢之弊，固止輕重銖兩之間，而非甚有所壅閼也。夫輕重數易則下擾，故惟五銖、開元最中焉，而開元迄今且傳之，謂通塞不關於是，不其然矣。故錢幣在周，利人者也；漢以後，利國者也。乃今日視周、漢，則又有大不然者。內而宗廟、聘享、乘輿、御府，外而宗藩、百官、邊鄙將士，有一弗藉於民者乎？正自總秷、米粟、藁絲，餘自關梁、市肆、鹽鐵，有一弗藉於官者乎？賦盡無益地，而泉府斂布之法難究詰矣；利盡無逸貨，而榷酤、市占之法旣舉矣。未豐其流，先恐竭其源。噫！此所謂時也。聖人不必於時，能必時之不違，則制而通之以法。法者，所以因時布利、庇民者也。若曰時不可，而并法廢焉，不亦以噎忘餐乎？我國家自太祖開天建極，創通寶者二，
translation_en:
… Their coinage problems were indeed merely a matter of slight differences in weight by zhu and liang, rather than severe obstruction in circulation. When weights are repeatedly altered, the people below are disturbed; thus only the Wuzhu and Kaiyuan coins struck the best balance, and the Kaiyuan coin has even been passed down to this day. To claim that smooth circulation or blockage has nothing to do with this is surely untrue. Therefore, in the Zhou dynasty, currency was designed to benefit the people; from the Han dynasty onward, it was designed to benefit the state.

Yet when we compare the present day with the Zhou and Han, the situation is vastly different again. Within the court—from the Imperial Ancestral Temple, diplomatic receptions and sacrificial offerings, to the imperial carriages and the Imperial Household Treasury—and outside the court—from the imperial clan princedoms and the hundred officials to the generals and soldiers on the frontiers—is there a single one that does not depend upon the people? Of the regular revenues—from bundled grain stalks, husked grain, unhusked grain, straw, and raw silk—and of the sundry revenues—from customs barriers and bridges, marketplace shops, salt, and iron—is there a single one that is not commandeered by the state? Land taxes have been exhausted with no additional land to tap, making the ancient Treasury of Coinage (Quanfu) system of collecting and distributing goods impossible to implement thoroughly; commercial profits have been exhausted with no untaxed goods remaining, as liquor monopolies and assessments on market assets have already been instituted. Before the stream has been made abundant, one already fears exhausting its source. Alas, this is what is meant by the circumstances of the times! The sage does not insist upon controlling the times, but can ensure that he does not act contrary to them, regulating and adapting to them through laws. Laws are the means by which one responds to the times to distribute benefits and shelter the people. If one says the times are unfavorable and consequently abandons the laws altogether, is that not like giving up eating for fear of choking?

Since our Grand Progenitor (Taizu) founded the empire and established the imperial standard, our dynasty created two types of circulating treasure (Tongbao) coins, …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
成
宣
孝
世四廟各更鑄以
鴻號項
主上允滇中按臣之請繼又允科臣之請議令
各省咸共鼓冶期在遐邇均布恭讀
明旨即阜化之道不啻竝周矣執事猶有宜民
虔始之慮毋乃患其行之難而求所以易
===
乎夫行之難何也其弊有二夫所以易而
行之何也其利有五
累朝制實初頒輦轂之民爭持入市燕齊晉宋
之地猶然鱗集江以南巨室或市藏之貧
者終未覩其式蓋誠病頒布弗廣矣而嘉
靖錢復有如所稱金背火漆鏇邊者鏇邊
捷便易折則金背格舊者日格而新者病
弗廣其弊一也富商大賈駕輕車挽巨艦
囊金篋中飈馳而電發攜錢則轉運維艱
punctuated: 成、宣、孝、世四廟，各更鑄以鴻號。項主上允滇中按臣之請，繼又允科臣之請，議令各省咸共鼓冶，期在遐邇均布。恭讀明旨，即阜化之道，不啻竝周矣。執事猶有宜民虔始之慮，毋乃患其行之難，而求所以易乎？夫行之難何也？其弊有二。夫所以易而行之何也？其利有五。累朝制實初頒，輦轂之民爭持入市，燕、齊、晉、宋之地，猶然鱗集；江以南，巨室或市藏之，貧者終未覩其式，蓋誠病頒布弗廣矣。而嘉靖錢復有如所稱「金背」、「火漆」、「鏇邊」者，鏇邊捷便易折，則金背格；舊者日格，而新者病弗廣，其弊一也。富商大賈，駕輕車，挽巨艦，囊金篋中，飈馳而電發；攜錢則轉運維艱，
translation_en:
…and during the four reigns of Chengzu, Xuanzong, Xiaozong, and Shizong, each recast coins bearing his grand reign title. Recently [項 for 頃], His Majesty approved the request of the Regional Inspector in Dian [Yunnan], and subsequently approved the request of a Supervising Secretary, deliberating to order every province to jointly smelt and cast coins, aiming for even distribution far and near. Reverently reading the clear imperial edict, the way of enriching and transforming the realm is nothing less than equal to that of the Zhou dynasty. Yet Your Excellency still harbors concerns about adapting to the people and being reverent at the outset—is it not because you worry about the difficulty of putting this into practice, and seek a way to make it easy?

Why is it difficult to put into practice? There are two abuses. And how can it be made easy to put into practice? There are five advantages.

When the standard coins [制實 for 制寶] of successive reigns were first issued, the people of the imperial capital vied to take them into the markets, and in the regions of Yan, Qi, Jin, and Song, they still gathered like fish scales. South of the Yangtze, however, great households might buy and hoard them, while the poor never even saw their design; this truly suffered from the fault of distribution not being wide enough. Moreover, among the Jiajing coins, there were those known as "golden-backed" (jinbei), "fire-lacquered" (huoqi), and "lathe-rimmed" (xuanbian). Because the lathe-rimmed ones were quick and convenient to make yet easily broken, the golden-backed ones were obstructed from circulation. As the old coins are daily obstructed and the new ones suffer from not being widely distributed—this is the first abuse.

Wealthy merchants and great traders drive light carriages and haul huge ships; when they pack silver in pouches and chests, they speed like a whirlwind and flash like lightning. If they carry copper cash, however, transport and shipment become exceedingly difficult…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
拘方阻廢彼行者不貿居者益不得致蓋
誠病用之弗流矣而通都姦擅自鑄僻壤
負山者間亦鎔冶以相規射民樂爲售而
不辨僞錢日溢而制錢復不致其弊二也
稽弊而亟反之何難焉夫王者布利豈必
持籌握算較短長於尺寸間哉計大於其
細則細可無論也圖遠於其近則近可無
論也時之所謂錢寡豈非以三金之難充
耶卓氏一遷虜即汶山鼓鑄至傾滇蜀之
===
富何者其源行也今銅山無論盡中國即
大行王屋亦間產銅誠洪禹湯即山之規
各就岑谷多礦道者以開而取盈我常橾
其餘而人亦須其不足是因地之利也俗
侈麗相高競以赤金爲玩具非鏴耶宛孔
氏繼啇嬴得過當至巨萬蓋南陽何者其
流不溢也今方申令銷廢器而愚民詐於
耳目以爲故常孰先之矣故莫如法征布
之遺意令天下以吏道貿道進者咸輸銅
punctuated: 拘方阻廢，彼行者不貿，居者益不得致，蓋誠病用之弗流矣。而通都姦擅自鑄，僻壤負山者間亦鎔冶以相規射，民樂爲售而不辨，僞錢日溢而制錢復不致，其弊二也。稽弊而亟反之，何難焉？夫王者布利，豈必持籌握算、較短長於尺寸間哉？計大於其細，則細可無論也；圖遠於其近，則近可無論也。時之所謂錢寡，豈非以三金之難充耶？卓氏一遷虜，即汶山鼓鑄，至傾滇、蜀之富，何者？其源行也。今銅山無論盡中國，即大行、王屋亦間產銅。誠洪禹、湯即山之規，各就岑谷多礦道者以開而取盈，我常橾其餘而人亦須其不足，是因地之利也。俗侈麗相高，競以赤金爲玩具，非鏴耶？宛孔氏繼啇嬴得過當，至巨萬，蓋南陽，何者？其流不溢也。今方申令銷廢器，而愚民詐於耳目，以爲故常，孰先之矣？故莫如法征布之遺意，令天下以吏道、貿道進者咸輸銅，
translation_en:
… restricted by regional boundaries and obstructed into disuse. When traveling merchants do not trade in them, resident folk are even less able to obtain them; this truly suffers from a failure of circulation. Meanwhile, illicit actors in great metropolises cast coins on their own authority, and those in remote regions backed against the mountains also occasionally smelt and cast to scheme for profit. The people gladly accept and pass them without distinguishing them, so counterfeit coins overflow day by day while official standard coins still do not arrive—this is the second abuse.

If we examine these abuses and urgently reverse them, what difficulty would there be? When a true king distributes economic benefits, why must he hold counting rods and calculate, comparing short and long down to the foot and inch? If one calculates the great from the small, the small need not be discussed; if one plans the distant from the near, the near need not be discussed. Is what the present age calls a scarcity of coins not due to the difficulty of supplying the three metals? The Zhuo 卓 clan were mere deported captives, yet by going to Mount Wen 汶山 to smelt and cast, they came to surpass the wealth of Dian 滇 and Shu 蜀. Why was this? Because their source was abundant [?]. Today, as for copper mountains, to say nothing of the whole of China, even the Taihang 太行 and Wangwu 王屋 mountains occasionally produce copper. If we truly expand the regulations of Yu 禹 and Tang 湯 for working the mountains, going to each peak and valley with many mine shafts to open them and extract a surplus, we will constantly hold the excess while others look to us for what they lack—this is taking advantage of the benefits of the earth.

Popular customs compete in extravagance and finery, vying to make playthings out of red metal [copper]—is this not fine metal [wasted] [?]? The Kong 孔 clan of Wan 宛, pursuing mercantile calculations and profits, gained extraordinary returns amounting to tens of millions, topping Nanyang 南陽. Why was this? Because their outflow did not spill over. Now orders have just been reiterated to melt down wasted copper utensils, yet the ignorant people are deceived by what their eyes and ears are used to [?], taking it as ordinary custom—who would be the first to comply? Therefore, nothing is better than emulating the ancient intent of levying cloth, ordering all in the Empire who advance through the paths of clerkships or commerce [?] to pay in copper…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
而會以值塞其廢之流而用恒因其廢是
導人之利也專官則責殷顧諸省地方常
千里夫千里遙制而冀血脉之聯貫難也
誠轉責郡貳楮市之出入考其通否亦周
官司市之義制利柄者也平價則衆趨顧
所平者金背鏇邊耳今民間猶多舊藏錢
而或雜於市淆也誠諭之首納官為之酬
復於鑪冶亦三官銷鑄之義一利孔者也
劉濞之鑄山也恃其宗疆而素封之駔儈
===
也成於倚市此私之由也故眞工大姦必
罪無赦豪右觸憲必鋤毋寬利不分也夫
舉五者之利而驅其弊弊驅則民宜民宜
則時從即不必奇羡於目前而息出息入
足下足上錢神不滯投金捐珠之化且坐
而致矣漢唐之盛何有哉故曰治天下者
利人者也非利於人者也厥或舍民之利
而日求所謂鑄之之法行之之方以籠天
下之財而曰吾以利國吾不信也
punctuated: 而會以值，塞其廢之流，而用恒因其廢，是導人之利也。專官則責殷，顧諸省地方常千里，夫千里遙制而冀血脉之聯貫，難也。誠轉責郡貳，楮市之出入考其通否，亦《周官》司市之義，制利柄者也。平價則衆趨，顧所平者金背、鏇邊耳。今民間猶多舊藏錢，而或雜於市，淆也。誠諭之首納，官為之酬，復於鑪冶，亦三官銷鑄之義，一利孔者也。劉濞之鑄山也，恃其宗疆；而素封之駔儈也，成於倚市，此私之由也。故眞工、大姦必罪無赦，豪右觸憲必鋤毋寬，利不分也。夫舉五者之利而驅其弊，弊驅則民宜，民宜則時從。即不必奇羡於目前，而息出息入，足下足上，錢神不滯，投金捐珠之化，且坐而致矣，漢、唐之盛何有哉？故曰：治天下者，利人者也，非利於人者也。厥或舍民之利，而日求所謂鑄之之法、行之之方，以籠天下之財，而曰「吾以利國」，吾不信也。
translation_en:
… and calculate its value; block the flow of wastefulness and constantly adapt usage from what is discarded—this is guiding the profit of the people.

Assigning dedicated officials makes responsibility weighty, yet the territory of each province often spans a thousand li; exercising remote control across a thousand li while hoping for the vital arteries of circulation to remain connected is difficult. If responsibility is instead delegated to the Vice Prefects (jun'er) to inspect the inflow and outflow of currency in the markets [?] and examine whether it circulates smoothly or not, this too accords with the principle of the Market Supervisor (sishi) in the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), thereby controlling the handle of profit.

Stabilizing prices causes the multitude to flock to the currency, yet what has been stabilized is merely the "gilt-backed" (jinbei) and "lathe-rimmed" (xuanbian) coins. Today among the people there are still many old hoarded coins, which at times get mixed into the markets, causing confusion. If we truly instruct the people to turn them in first, with the authorities compensating them and returning the metal to the furnaces and smelters, this too accords with the principle of melting and casting by the Three Offices (sanguan) of the Han, thereby unifying the channels of profit.

When Liu Pi 劉濞 minted coins from the mountains, he relied on his imperial clan status and territory; and as for the "uncrowned lords" (sufeng, wealthy commoners) acting as brokers, they succeeded by leaning on the markets. Such are the origins of illicit minting. Therefore, skilled artisans and great villains must be punished without pardon, and powerful families who violate the law must be rooted out without leniency, so that profit is not divided.

Now, if we promote these five advantages and drive away their abuses, once the abuses are driven away, the people will be accommodated; once the people are accommodated, the times will follow suit. Even if there is no extraordinary surplus right before our eyes, as wealth flows out and in, sufficing both those below and those above, the spirit of money (qianshen) will not stagnate, and the moral transformation of casting away gold and discarding pearls will be achieved while sitting at ease—what difficulty would there be in matching the flourishing ages of Han and Tang?

Therefore it is said: he who governs the world benefits others; he does not profit from others. If someone sets aside what benefits the people and daily seeks out so-called methods of minting and ways of circulating currency in order to monopolize the wealth of the world, while claiming, "I do this to benefit the state," I do not believe him.

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
第三問
同考試官教諭葉　批〔士子能明象緯者甚少是篇考究詳確迥出衆作可以覘所養矣〕
景　明
考試官學正梅　批〔發揮明悉〕
考試官教授朱　批〔才識俱可〕
曆象之所係豈不重哉易賁之象曰觀乎
天文以察時變而革之象則曰澤中有火
革君子以治曆明時夫天下之可革者亦
===
多矣而聖人必以以曆爲言者得無以天時
人事相爲感招而時之所係於治者重也
時不可以易知而其變則每每洩於日月
星辰之象觀變而時可知觀曆而變可知
曆之所係於時者重也顧其爲道高遠而
難窺其數微渺而莫可詰其參差盈縮之
態又時出而不可窮昔人謂事之易差者
莫如曆不可不脩者亦莫如曆信矣曆象
之所係又豈可易言哉太史公推曆之始
punctuated:
第三問

同考試官教諭葉批：〔士子能明象緯者甚少，是篇考究詳確，迥出衆作，可以覘所養矣。〕

景明

考試官學正梅批：〔發揮明悉。〕

考試官教授朱批：〔才識俱可。〕

曆象之所係，豈不重哉！《易》〈賁〉之〈象〉曰：「觀乎天文，以察時變。」而〈革〉之〈象〉則曰：「澤中有火，革；君子以治曆明時。」夫天下之可革者亦多矣，而聖人必以以曆爲言者，得無以天時、人事相爲感招，而時之所係於治者重也？時不可以易知，而其變則每每洩於日月星辰之象。觀變而時可知，觀曆而變可知，曆之所係於時者重也。顧其爲道高遠而難窺，其數微渺而莫可詰，其參差盈縮之態，又時出而不可窮。昔人謂「事之易差者莫如曆，不可不脩者亦莫如曆」，信矣！曆象之所係，又豈可易言哉！太史公推曆之始，
translation_en:
Third Question

Associate Examiner, County Director of Studies Ye, comments: [Very few scholars are able to understand astronomical phenomena and the celestial bodies. This essay investigates them in detail and with precision, standing far above the crowd of compositions; from it one can observe the depth of his cultivation.]

Jing Ming 景明

Examiner, Subprefectural Director of Studies Mei, comments: [The exposition is clear and thorough.]

Examiner, Prefectural Director of Studies Zhu, comments: [Both talent and insight are commendable.]

How could that upon which the calendar and astronomical phenomena depend not be of great importance! In the Book of Changes (Yi), the commentary [Tuan, here written Xiang] on the hexagram Bi ("Grace") says: "Observe the patterns of heaven in order to examine the changes of the seasons." And the Image commentary (Xiang) on the hexagram Ge ("Revolution") says: "In the midst of the marsh there is fire: Revolution. Thus the noble man regulates the calendar and makes clear the seasons." Now, the things in the world that are subject to revolution and reform are indeed many, yet the sages必ず spoke of the calendar [here]. Could it not be because the seasons of heaven and the affairs of men mutually respond to and summon one another, so that what the seasons entail for governance is of great weight? The seasons cannot be easily known, yet their changes are invariably revealed in the phenomena of the sun, moon, stars, and celestial markers. By observing the changes, the seasons can be known; by observing the calendar, the changes can be known. Thus, what the calendar entails for the seasons is of great weight. However, its Way is lofty, distant, and difficult to peer into; its numerical principles are subtle, abstruse, and impossible to fully fathom; and its uneven states of waxing and waning emerge from time to time and cannot be exhausted. When men of the past said, "Among affairs that easily fall into error, none is like the calendar; and among those that cannot go unrevised, none is like the calendar," it was truly so! How, then, can that upon which the calendar and astronomical phenomena depend be spoken of lightly! When the Grand Historian (Taishigong, Sima Qian) traced the beginnings of the calendar, …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
謂神農以前尚已黃帝迎日推測建立五
行起消息正閏餘蓋是時始有曆云其後
脩廢靡常治亂不爽姑無論已見於書所
稱者欽若昊天敬授人時非堯之所以命
羲和者乎在璿璣玉衡以齊七政非舜之
所以先時度者乎協用五紀非箕子之所
以陳於武王者乎三聖人之致謹於天道
也如此非徒以奉天也所以宜民也其宜
民也正所以善治也秦不師古無足道者
===
迨漢興潭天儀之法出焉其制始於漢元
封其法最爲精密朱元晦謂古必有其法
遭秦而滅而楊子雲以爲落下閎營之鮮
於妄人度之耿中丞象之幾幾乎莫之能
違固璣璿玉衡之遺意而天之所不能外
也三代而下說天文者不下數十家而圖
書之作亦頗稱浩翰其間占驗候卜之法
類皆互有得失而日躔月離日法斗分氣
盈朔虛之數往往不能無謬大都漢自張
punctuated: 謂神農以前尚已，黃帝迎日推測，建立五行，起消息，正閏餘，蓋是時始有曆云。其後脩廢靡常，治亂不爽，姑無論已。見於《書》所稱者：「欽若昊天，敬授人時」，非堯之所以命羲和者乎？「在璿璣玉衡，以齊七政」，非舜之所以先時度者乎？「協用五紀」，非箕子之所以陳於武王者乎？三聖人之致謹於天道也如此，非徒以奉天也，所以宜民也；其宜民也，正所以善治也。秦不師古，無足道者。迨漢興，潭天儀之法出焉。其制始於漢元封，其法最爲精密。朱元晦謂古必有其法，遭秦而滅；而楊子雲以爲落下閎營之，鮮於妄人度之，耿中丞象之，幾幾乎莫之能違，固璣璿玉衡之遺意，而天之所不能外也。三代而下，說天文者不下數十家，而圖書之作亦頗稱浩翰。其間占驗候卜之法，類皆互有得失，而日躔、月離、日法、斗分、氣盈、朔虛之數，往往不能無謬。大都漢自張
translation_en:
… says that before Shennong the past is too remote to speak of, and that the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) observed the sun to make calculations, established the Five Phases, initiated the waxing and waning of yin and yang, and rectified the intercalary remainder—it was around this time that the calendar is said to have begun. Thereafter, its revision and neglect were inconstant, unfailingly mirroring order and disorder, though we may leave that aside for now. As for what is recorded in the Book of Documents (Shu): Was not "reverently following vast Heaven and respectfully bestowing the seasons on the people" Yao's charge to Xi and He? Was not "examining the jade-adorned sighting tube to align the Seven Regulators" how Shun gave priority to the measures of time? And was not "harmoniously employing the Five Arrangers" what the Viscount of Ji (Jizi) set forth to King Wu? That the three sages exercised such extreme care regarding the Way of Heaven was not merely to serve Heaven, but to suit the needs of the people; and suiting the needs of the people was precisely how they achieved good governance. The Qin did not model itself on antiquity and is not worth mentioning.

When the Han arose, the method of the celestial sphere (huntianyi [transcribed as tantianyi]) emerged. Its system began in the Yuanfeng era (110–105 BCE) of the Han, and its method was most precise. Zhu Xi (Zhu Yuanhui 朱元晦) held that antiquity must have possessed this method before it perished under the Qin; whereas Yang Xiong (Yang Ziyun 楊子雲) stated that Luoxia Hong 落下閎 constructed it, Xianyu Wangren 鮮于妄人 measured it, and Palace Aide to the Censor-in-chief Geng Shouchang (Geng Zhongcheng 耿中丞) modeled the celestial phenomena with it, approaching such perfection that nothing could deviate from it. Indeed, it preserved the legacy of the jade-adorned sighting tube, from which Heaven itself cannot depart. From the Three Dynasties onward, those who expounded on astronomy numbered no fewer than several dozen schools, and the charts and writings produced were also quite vast. Among them, methods of prognostication, verification, observation, and divination generally each had their merits and faults, while the figures for the solar trajectory, lunar path, denominator of the day-fraction (rifa), dipper fraction (doufen), solar surplus (qiying), and lunar deficit (shuoxu) were often not without error. Broadly speaking, in the Han, from Zhang…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
蒼劉歆而下曆凡五變而莫善於太初鄧
平輩所造也其說本於黄鍾其數起於八
十一步之以前歷而歲逢攝提格首之以
建星而日得甲子日月如合壁五星如連
珠晦朔弦望不忒其序而一十七家之曆
廢矣唐自傅仁均李淳風而下曆凡八變
而莫善於大衍僧一行所作也其法本於
天地之二中其數始於冬至之中氣以卦
氣定七十二候以中星正二十四氣天數
===
始於一地數始於二彼則合二始以位剛
柔天數終於九地數終於十彼則合二終
以正餘閏章蔀紀元莫非易義而二十三
家之曆廢矣此二曆古今極稱精密而要
之皆根柢渾天而作者也梁令瓚李淳風
之輩其法非不密而實囿於二曆之中矣
自是而後若欽天應天等曆非不有可取
者而惟勝國之授時曆乃郭守敬成之廣
景測以稽運行取中數以爲曆本元史所
punctuated: 蒼、劉歆而下，曆凡五變，而莫善於《太初》，鄧平輩所造也。其說本於黄鍾，其數起於八十一，步之以前歷，而歲逢攝提格；首之以建星，而日得甲子。日月如合壁，五星如連珠，晦朔弦望不忒其序，而一十七家之曆廢矣。唐自傅仁均、李淳風而下，曆凡八變，而莫善於《大衍》，僧一行所作也。其法本於天地之二中，其數始於冬至之中氣，以卦氣定七十二候，以中星正二十四氣。天數始於一，地數始於二，彼則合二始以位剛柔；天數終於九，地數終於十，彼則合二終以正餘閏。章、蔀、紀、元，莫非《易》義，而二十三家之曆廢矣。此二曆古今極稱精密，而要之皆根柢渾天而作者也。梁令瓚、李淳風之輩，其法非不密，而實囿於二曆之中矣。自是而後，若《欽天》、《應天》等曆，非不有可取者，而惟勝國之《授時曆》，乃郭守敬成之。廣景測以稽運行，取中數以爲曆本，《元史》所
translation_en:
… Cang 張蒼 and Liu Xin 劉歆 onward, the calendar underwent five reforms in all, and none was better than the Grand Inception Calendar (Taichu li 太初曆), which was constructed by Deng Ping 鄧平 and his colleagues. Its theory was grounded in the Yellow Bell (huangzhong 黄鍾) pitch-pipe, and its numerical base began with eighty-one. Calculating back through previous eras, the year coincided with the shetige 攝提格 [yin 寅] Jupiter station; starting it at the Establishment Star (Jianxing 建星), the day fell upon jiazi 甲子. The sun and moon were like joined jade discs, and the five planets were like strung pearls; the last day of the month, the new moon, the quarter moons, and the full moon did not err in their sequence, and the calendars of the seventeen schools were discarded.

In the Tang dynasty, from Fu Renjun 傅仁均 and Li Chunfeng 李淳風 onward, the calendar underwent eight reforms in all, and none was better than the Great Expansion Calendar (Dayan li 大衍曆), which was created by the monk Yixing 一行. Its method was grounded in the two central numbers of Heaven and Earth [five and six], and its calculations began with the medial qi (zhongqi 中氣) of the winter solstice. It used the hexagram qi (guaqi 卦氣) to determine the seventy-two pentads (hou 候), and used the culminating stars to rectify the twenty-four solar terms (qi 氣). The numbers of Heaven begin with one, and the numbers of Earth begin with two—he combined these two beginnings to position the firm and the yielding; the numbers of Heaven end with nine, and the numbers of Earth end with ten—he combined these two endings to rectify the remainders and intercalations. The cycle of nineteen years (zhang 章), the cycle of seventy-six years (bu 蔀), the cycle of 1,520 years (ji 紀), and the grand cycle of 4,560 years (yuan 元) were all drawn from the principles of the Book of Changes (Yi 易), and the calendars of the twenty-three schools were discarded.

These two calendars have been praised from antiquity to the present as supremely precise, and in essence both were created on the foundation of the Celestial Sphere (huntian 渾天) theory. As for men like Liang Lingzan 梁令瓚 and Li Chunfeng, their methods were not imprecise, yet in reality they remained confined within the scope of these two calendars. From that time onward, calendars such as the Reverent Heaven (Qintian 欽天) and Responsive to Heaven (Yingtian 應天) were not without merits, yet it was uniquely the Season-Granting Calendar (Shoushi li 授時曆) of the conquered dynasty [the Yuan] that was brought to completion by Guo Shoujing 郭守敬. He broadened gnomon shadow measurements to verify celestial movements and adopted median values as the fundamental basis of the calendar. What the History of the Yuan (Yuanshi 元史) …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
謂自古至今推驗之精無出於此信不誣
矣是其所傳述莫非象衡之遺而推步則
得於獨見之真也是故以察二曜則日之
行每日遶地一周凡行三百六十五度四
分度之一積三百六十五日九百四十分
日之二百三十五而與天會是爲一歲月
之行每日遶地一周凡不及天十三度十
九分度之七積二十九日九百四十分日
之四百九十九而與日會是爲一月而遲
===
速因之而占矣以驗四候則日與天會一
歲一次而二十四氣由之以生然二十四
氣凡三百六十五日有奇而周則是於三
百六十之外盈五日也月與天會一歲十
二次而十二朔由之以生然十二朔凡三
百五十四日有奇而周則是於三百六十
之中虛五日也而消息因之以考矣日何
爲有法也一日爲十二辰又細分爲百刻
而又細分之則如四分曆以爲九百四十
punctuated: 謂「自古至今，推驗之精，無出於此」，信不誣矣。是其所傳述，莫非象衡之遺，而推步則得於獨見之真也。是故以察二曜，則日之行，每日遶地一周，凡行三百六十五度四分度之一，積三百六十五日九百四十分日之二百三十五而與天會，是爲一歲；月之行，每日遶地一周，凡不及天十三度十九分度之七，積二十九日九百四十分日之四百九十九而與日會，是爲一月，而遲速因之而占矣。以驗四候，則日與天會，一歲一次，而二十四氣由之以生；然二十四氣凡三百六十五日有奇而周，則是於三百六十之外，盈五日也。月與天會，一歲十二次，而十二朔由之以生；然十二朔凡三百五十四日有奇而周，則是於三百六十之中，虛五日也，而消息因之以考矣。日何爲有法也？一日爲十二辰，又細分爲百刻，而又細分之，則如《四分曆》以爲九百四十、
translation_en: …states that "from antiquity to the present, in the precision of its calculations and verifications, none has surpassed this," it is truly no exaggeration. Thus, what they transmitted was nothing other than the legacy of the sighting tube and armillary sphere, while their astronomical calculations were attained through the truth of their own unique insights. Therefore, in observing the two luminaries: as for the movement of the sun, each day it circles the earth once, traveling in all 365 and 1/4 degrees, accumulating 365 and 235/940 days to meet with the heavens, which constitutes one solar year; as for the movement of the moon, each day it circles the earth once, falling short of the heavens by 13 and 7/19 degrees in all, accumulating 29 and 499/940 days to meet with the sun, which constitutes one lunation—and slowness and swiftness are thereby divined from this. In verifying the four seasons: the sun meets with the heavens once a year, and the twenty-four solar terms are generated from this; yet the twenty-four solar terms take 365 days and a fraction in all to complete a cycle, which is an excess of five days beyond 360. The moon meets with the heavens [or rather, the sun] twelve times a year, and the twelve new moons are generated from this; yet the twelve new moons take 354 days and a fraction in all to complete a cycle, which is a deficit of five days within 360—and waxing and waning are thereby examined from this. Why does the day have a divisor (ri fa)? One day is divided into twelve double-hours, and further subdivided into one hundred quarters (ke), and when subdivided yet again, it is as the Quarter-Remainder Calendar (Sifen li) takes it to be 940,…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
太初曆以爲八十一大衍曆以爲三千四
十是也蓋取其便於步推氣朔而已斗何
爲有分也斗柄指十二辰而又細分爲三
十四度而又細分之則如太初以爲三百
八十五大衍以爲七百七十九是也蓋取
其便於觀候星辰而已有盈虛則有閏餘
蓋定歲不可不係朔虛之數而節氣不可
不數閏餘之月故三年一閏五年再閏積
十九年七閏而氣朔又同日也然夏九月
===
辰弗集房周十一月大火西流豈非失閏
之過乎有日躔則有歲差蓋天道平運而
舒則漸差而西日道內轉而縮則漸差而
東故皇極曆以爲七十五年差一度大衍
曆以爲八十三年差一度也然謂陰陽之
運隨動而差差而不已遂與曆錯豈非已
往之驗乎噫天地之數其妙不測者常在
於秒忽毫釐之間而推移盈縮亦有時而
不齊不可以一定求之者是以爲曆者其
punctuated: 《太初曆》以爲八十一，《大衍曆》以爲三千四十是也。蓋取其便於步推氣朔而已。斗何爲有分也？斗柄指十二辰，而又細分爲三十四度，而又細分之，則如《太初》以爲三百八十五，《大衍》以爲七百七十九是也。蓋取其便於觀候星辰而已。有盈虛，則有閏餘。蓋定歲不可不係朔虛之數，而節氣不可不數閏餘之月。故三年一閏，五年再閏，積十九年七閏，而氣朔又同日也。然夏九月辰弗集房，周十一月大火西流，豈非失閏之過乎？有日躔，則有歲差。蓋天道平運而舒，則漸差而西；日道內轉而縮，則漸差而東。故《皇極曆》以爲七十五年差一度，《大衍曆》以爲八十三年差一度也。然謂陰陽之運，隨動而差，差而不已，遂與曆錯，豈非已往之驗乎？噫！天地之數，其妙不測者，常在於秒忽毫釐之間，而推移盈縮，亦有時而不齊，不可以一定求之者。是以爲曆者，其
translation_en: … the Grand Inception Calendar (Taichu li) took it as eighty-one, and the Great Expansion Calendar (Dayan li) took it as three thousand and forty. This is simply adopted for convenience in calculating the solar terms and new moons. Why does the Dipper have fractional divisions (doufen)? The handle of the Dipper points to the twelve zodiacal positions, which are further subdivided into thirty-four degrees [?], and when subdivided even further, the Grand Inception Calendar took the denominator as three hundred and eighty-five, and the Great Expansion Calendar took it as seven hundred and seventy-nine. This is simply adopted for convenience in observing the stars and celestial bodies. Because there are solar surpluses and lunar deficiencies, there is an intercalary remainder. Determining the year cannot but take into account the days of lunar deficiency, and fixing the solar terms cannot but reckon the months formed from the intercalary remainder. Therefore, there is one intercalary month in three years, two intercalary months in five years, and accumulating seven intercalary months over nineteen years brings the solar term and the new moon back to the same day. Yet in the ninth month during the Xia dynasty, the sun and moon did not meet harmoniously in the Room (Fang) lodge, and in the eleventh month during the Zhou dynasty, the Great Fire star (Antares) was still declining westward—was this not the fault of failing to insert intercalary months? Because the sun has its orbital progression (richan), there is the precession of the equinoxes (suicha). The way of Heaven revolves evenly and extends outward, gradually shifting toward the west; the path of the sun turns inward and contracts, gradually shifting toward the east. Thus the Supreme Ultimate Calendar (Huangji li) held that it shifts by one degree in seventy-five years, while the Great Expansion Calendar held that it shifts by one degree in eighty-three years. Yet the saying that the movement of yin and yang shifts along with its motion, and shifting endlessly, eventually falls out of step with the calendar—is this not proven by past experience? Alas! In the numerical principles of Heaven and Earth, what is wondrous and unfathomable always lies within the tiniest fractions—seconds,絲, hairs, and hundredths—and their shifting, waxing, and waning are also at times irregular and cannot be sought through fixed rules. Therefore, when calendar-makers construct a calendar, at its…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
始未必不密其後多踈而不合者亦理之
自然數之不得不然耳神而明之不亦存
乎其人哉惟我
國家承天膺曆
高皇帝神智中啓凡象緯星度靡不周知惟時
占天有臺造曆有官推步有法以釐百工
而興庶務其制國爲精且密矣考之當時
博士元統言於
上曰
===
國家承運以來曆雖以大統爲名而積分猶
授時之數授時曆法以元至元辛巳爲曆
元至今洪武甲子積一百四年以曆法推
之得三億七千六百一十九萬九千七百
七十五分經云大約七十年而差一度每
歲差一分五十秒辛巳至今年遠數盈漸
差天度擬合脩改夫當元統上言歲在甲
子而已云然矧今又曆幾甲子矣其年愈
遠其數愈多其所差者當益甚也茲遇
punctuated: 始未必不密，其後多踈而不合者，亦理之自然，數之不得不然耳。神而明之，不亦存乎其人哉？惟我國家承天膺曆，高皇帝神智中啓，凡象緯星度，靡不周知。惟時占天有臺，造曆有官，推步有法，以釐百工而興庶務，其制固爲精且密矣。考之當時，博士元統言於上曰：「國家承運以來，曆雖以《大統》爲名，而積分猶《授時》之數。《授時曆》法以元至元辛巳爲曆元，至今洪武甲子，積一百四年。以曆法推之，得三億七千六百一十九萬九千七百七十五分。經云：『大約七十年而差一度，每歲差一分五十秒。』辛巳至今，年遠數盈，漸差天度，擬合脩改。」夫當元統上言，歲在甲子，而已云然；矧今又曆幾甲子矣，其年愈遠，其數愈多，其所差者當益甚也。茲遇
translation_en:
…beginning are not necessarily imprecise, yet later on they mostly grow loose and fail to match; this too is simply the natural course of principle and the unavoidable outcome of mathematical calculation. To comprehend this with神-like subtlety and illuminate it—does that not depend upon the right person?

When our Dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven and assumed the succession, the High Emperor (Gao Huangdi 高皇帝, i.e., the Hongwu Emperor), with his divinely inspired wisdom awakening from within, thoroughly understood all celestial phenomena, planetary motions, and stellar degrees. At that time, there was an observatory for observing the heavens, officials for compiling the calendar, and methods for astronomical calculation, so as to regulate the hundred artisans and make all state affairs flourish. Its system was indeed [reading 固 for 國] both refined and precise! Examining the records of that time, the Erudite (boshi) Yuan Tong 元統 spoke to the throne, saying: "Since the Dynasty received the Mandate, although the calendar is named the Great Concordance (Datong 大統), its accumulated fractions still follow the figures of the Season-Granting (Shoushi 授時) system. The Season-Granting Calendar method took the xinsi year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan dynasty (1281) as its calendrical epoch. Down to the present jiazi year of the Hongwu era (1384), one hundred and four years have accumulated. Calculating by the calendrical method, this yields 376,199,775 fractional units (fen). The canon states: 'Approximately every seventy years there is a discrepancy of one degree, with an annual precession of one fen and fifty miao.' From the xinsi year to the present, the years have grown distant and the figures have accumulated to excess, gradually diverging from the celestial degrees; I propose that it ought to be revised." Now, when Yuan Tong submitted his words, the year was only at that first jiazi (1384), and yet he already spoke thus; how much more so today, when several more jiazi cycles have elapsed! As the years grow ever more distant and the figures ever more numerous, the resulting discrepancies must be even more severe. Now, encountering…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
聖明在上敬天勤民孜孜不怠天下臣民莫不
快覩矣則講求曆法以昭一代大典非其
時與夫釐正於千百世之下則當考究於
千百世之前自古造曆者必先立元是以
黄帝以來立元雖若不同而皆準度於甲
子所謂夜半冬至而日月五星皆會焉以
爲曆始此歷代宗旨也先民有言曆元止
據目前考驗無證其術失之淺上推開闢
冥測鴻濛其術近乎迂必也用太史公三
===
紀大備之法范史紀元之目推上元甲子
四千五百餘年則其時不遠不近矣斯言
也獨觀其深者哉然此非易易也愚觀今
曆數之職太輕而疇人子弟操其術授受
若藝匠然蓋止能循其已往之筭而未能
通其變於推移之外安望其曆之興耶宜
重其職精其選仍博訪巖穴通習天文之
士而遇之以禮其一在世業如漢馬遷歷
朝太史授受有自律曆精專可也其次在
punctuated: 聖明在上，敬天勤民，孜孜不怠，天下臣民莫不快覩矣。則講求曆法，以昭一代大典，非其時與？夫釐正於千百世之下，則當考究於千百世之前。自古造曆者，必先立元，是以黄帝以來，立元雖若不同，而皆準度於甲子，所謂「夜半冬至，而日月五星皆會焉，以爲曆始」，此歷代宗旨也。先民有言：「曆元止據目前，考驗無證，其術失之淺；上推開闢，冥測鴻濛，其術近乎迂。必也用太史公三紀大備之法、范史紀元之目，推上元甲子四千五百餘年，則其時不遠不近矣。」斯言也，獨觀其深者哉！然此非易易也。愚觀今曆數之職太輕，而疇人子弟操其術，授受若藝匠然。蓋止能循其已往之筭，而未能通其變於推移之外，安望其曆之興耶？宜重其職，精其選，仍博訪巖穴通習天文之士，而遇之以禮。其一在世業，如漢馬遷歷朝太史，授受有自，律曆精專，可也；其次在
translation_en: … His Sacred Majesty is on the throne, revering Heaven and laboring diligently for the people, untiring in his devotion; among the officials and subjects across the realm, there is none who does not rejoice to witness this. Is it not then the very time to investigate and master the calendrical methods so as to illuminate the great institutions of our era? Now, to rectify the calendar after hundreds and thousands of generations, one must examine into the past across hundreds and thousands of generations. Since antiquity, those who construct calendars must first establish an epoch (yuan). Thus, since the time of the Yellow Emperor, although the establishment of epochs has seemed to differ, all have taken the jiazi cycle as their standard of measurement—what is referred to as "when the winter solstice falls at midnight, and the sun, moon, and five planets all conjoin there, taking this as the beginning of the calendar." This has been the fundamental principle of successive dynasties. A predecessor once said: "If the calendrical epoch relies solely on the immediate present, its verification lacks corroborating evidence, and the method errs in being too shallow; if it extrapolates back to the creation of the world, blindly fathoming the primordial chaos, the method comes close to being impractical. What is necessary is to employ the Grand Scribe's (Taishigong, Sima Qian) method of the great completion of three eras (sanji) and the Epoch-Recording (Jiyuan) rubric in Fan Ye's History of the Later Han (Fan shi), extrapolating back to a High Epoch (shangyuan) jiazi of some four thousand five hundred years; then the time frame is neither too distant nor too near." Do these words alone not perceive the matter in its depth! Yet this is by no means an easy task. In my humble view, the offices in charge of calendrical calculation today are held in too light esteem, and the descendants of hereditary astronomers (chouren) practice their art, passing it down as if they were mere artisans. Since they can only follow the calculations of the past and are unable to comprehend transformations beyond routine shifts, how can one hope for calendrical science to flourish? It is fitting to give greater weight to their offices and refine their selection, while also searching broadly among rustic retreats for scholars thoroughly versed in astronomy and treating them with ritual courtesy. First, priority lies in hereditary specialization: if, like Sima Qian of the Han and the Grand Scribes (Taishi) of successive courts, their transmission has an established origin and their mastery of harmonics and calendar-making is refined and dedicated, that will do. Second, it lies…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
於明經如詔御史大夫倪寬與博士共議
可也其次在於通筭如洛下閎陰陽歷朔
先後脗合可也而又得善立差法如邵雍
者以任之曆其有興乎若究其本則統於
人君之一心焉堯有曆象四時所由定而
允恭執兢堯心有曆象矣舜有璣衡七政
所由齊而惟時惟幾舜心有璣衡矣五紀
協用皇極所由建而敬聖怠義勝欲武心
有五紀矣是數聖人者皆以至誠之心而
契造化之原有不徒恃乎象數之爲者時
雍化洽所宜然也
===
皇上聰明天啓
睿智日新自强不息則體乾行健厚德載物
則配地無疆以陰陽爲端則舒慘中節以
四時爲柄則生息不窮以日星爲紀則照
臨無外是謂一天人賛化育曆數之源固
以一心而契其祕矣感召所在天且弗違
而況於人乎當必有精於其數又精於其
punctuated: 於明經，如詔御史大夫倪寬與博士共議，可也；其次在於通筭，如洛下閎陰陽歷朔先後脗合，可也；而又得善立差法如邵雍者以任之，曆其有興乎？若究其本，則統於人君之一心焉。堯有曆象，四時所由定，而「允恭執兢」，堯心有曆象矣；舜有璣衡，七政所由齊，而「惟時惟幾」，舜心有璣衡矣；五紀協用，皇極所由建，而「敬聖怠，義勝欲」，武心有五紀矣。是數聖人者，皆以至誠之心，而契造化之原，有不徒恃乎象數之爲者，時雍化洽，所宜然也。皇上聰明天啓，睿智日新。自强不息，則體乾行健；厚德載物，則配地無疆。以陰陽爲端，則舒慘中節；以四時爲柄，則生息不窮；以日星爲紀，則照臨無外。是謂一天人、賛化育，曆數之源，固以一心而契其祕矣。感召所在，天且弗違，而況於人乎？當必有精於其數，又精於其
translation_en:
… lies in mastery of the Classics, such as ordering the Censor-in-chief Ni Kuan 倪寬 to deliberate jointly with the Erudites—that will do; next, it lies in mastery of calculation, such as Luoxia Hong 洛下閎 making the succession of yin and yang, calendar and new moons fit together seamlessly—that will do; and if we further obtain someone skilled at establishing methods for calculating precession like Shao Yong 邵雍 to entrust with the task, will the calendar not flourish?

Yet if we examine its root, it is unified within the single mind of the ruler. Yao 堯 had calendrical calculations and astronomical observations by which the four seasons were determined, yet in being "sincerely courteous and holding fast to trembling caution," Yao's mind itself possessed the calendrical calculations and astronomical observations; Shun 舜 had the armillary sphere and sighting tube (jiheng 璣衡) by which the Seven Governors were regulated, yet in "attending to the timely and the subtle," Shun's mind itself possessed the armillary sphere and sighting tube; the harmonious use of the Five Regulators was that by which the August Ultimate was established, yet in "reverence overcoming [聖 for 勝?] indolence and righteousness overcoming desire," King Wu's 武 mind itself possessed the Five Regulators. All these several sages, through a mind of utmost sincerity, tallied with the source of creation and transformation; they did not merely rely on the operations of images and numbers, which is rightly why their eras were harmonious and their transformations all-pervading.

His Majesty, with intelligence conferred by Heaven and sagely wisdom daily renewed, ceaselessly strengthens himself, thereby embodying the vigorous movement of Heaven (Qian 乾); with generous virtue he sustains all things, thereby matching the boundless nature of Earth. Taking yin and yang as his beginnings, leniency and severity hit the proper measure; taking the four seasons as his handle of authority, growth and rest are inexhaustible; taking the sun and stars as his regulators, his illumination leaves nothing outside. This is what is meant by unifying Heaven and Man and assisting the transforming and nourishing powers of nature; the source of calendrical calculation has truly tallied with its mysteries through his single mind. Where his moral influence summons a response, even Heaven does not go against him—how much less so men! Surely there will be those who are thoroughly versed in its numbers and also thoroughly versed in its …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
理者以屑其職而曆不患其不興矣
第四問
劉敏寬
同考試官教諭王　批〔鹽政關晉中大計士子皆勦習舊說此篇條陳詳悉如指諸掌是獨擅策場者取之〕
考試官學正梅　批〔才思充贍而識見尤出人意表〕
考試官教授朱　批〔條答明確宜錄以式〕
天地有自然之利而所以生之者貴裕其
源天下無不弊之法而所以祛之者貴通
===
其變何則天之生財以為民也國之置法
亦以民也財本裕矣而生之者未盡其道
何以資之而不窮法未善矣而操之者或
泥其常何以行之而無弊蓋國依於商患
不利商耳利於商而不利於國者否也商
依於民患不便民耳便於民而不便於商
者否也是故因其勢而利導之以裕生財
之源酌其宜而變通之以去害財之弊寧
非今日之急務哉愚請言之而執事終聽
punctuated:
理者以屑其職，而曆不患其不興矣。

第四問
劉敏寬
同考試官教諭王　批〔鹽政關晉中大計，士子皆勦習舊說，此篇條陳詳悉，如指諸掌，是獨擅策場者，取之。〕
考試官學正梅　批〔才思充贍，而識見尤出人意表。〕
考試官教授朱　批〔條答明確，宜錄以式。〕

天地有自然之利，而所以生之者貴裕其源；天下無不弊之法，而所以祛之者貴通其變。何則？天之生財以為民也，國之置法亦以民也。財本裕矣，而生之者未盡其道，何以資之而不窮？法未善矣，而操之者或泥其常，何以行之而無弊？蓋國依於商，患不利商耳，利於商而不利於國者否也；商依於民，患不便民耳，便於民而不便於商者否也。是故因其勢而利導之，以裕生財之源；酌其宜而變通之，以去害財之弊，寧非今日之急務哉？愚請言之，而執事終聽
translation_en:
…principles to undertake [?] the office, and there will be no need to worry that the calendar will not flourish.

Fourth Policy Question
Liu Minkuan 劉敏寬
Associate Examiner, Instructor Wang 王 comments: [Salt administration concerns the grand fiscal plans of Shanxi. The candidates all plagiarize and repeat old theories, whereas this essay sets out its points in thorough detail, as clearly as pointing to one's own palm. He alone excels in the policy session; select it.]
Examiner, Subprefectural Instructor Mei 梅 comments: [His talent and thought are abundant and rich, and his insight especially surpasses expectations.]
Examiner, Prefectural Instructor Zhu 朱 comments: [His itemized responses are clear and precise; it ought to be recorded as a model.]

Heaven and Earth possess natural resources of profit, and the way to generate them values enriching their source; the realm has no law that does not develop abuses, and the way to dispel them values adapting to changing circumstances. Why is this? Heaven generates wealth for the sake of the people, and the state establishes laws also for the sake of the people. When wealth is inherently abundant, yet those who generate it have not exhausted the proper way, how can one draw upon it without exhaustion? When a law is not yet perfected [or: inherently good], yet those who administer it perhaps cling rigidly to routine, how can it be put into practice without abuse? Indeed, the state relies upon merchants, and the only worry is failing to profit the merchants; there is no such thing as profiting the merchants without profiting the state. Merchants rely upon the people, and the only worry is failing to convenience the people; there is no such thing as conveniencing the people without conveniencing the merchants. Therefore, to follow the natural tendency of circumstances and guide them profitably so as to enrich the source of generating wealth, and to weigh what is appropriate and adapt flexibly so as to remove the abuses that harm wealth—is this not the urgent task of today? I beg to speak of it, and may Your Excellency hear me out to the end…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
焉夫解之有池舊矣歷代之張弛沿革愚
未暇悉也昔所稱爲瑩潔如玉卦美如穀
亦宇內之所共蝓也愚不暇論也
祖宗時額鹽僅十萬耳至嘉靖中始增至十九
萬有奇全晉關洛梁鄧之閒皆其轉輸之
所也二百年來公私俱足在商人未嘗以
山徑巉嶮稱難在三省未嘗以解鹽苦惡
爲病何也法一而志定也自隆慶辛未雨
決池防池水肆溢鹽不結聚當事者謂
===
國計不可負始爲澆曬之術蓋以人力勝天
時也然而硝與鹽淆不能一一而析之也
有姦商者出焉乘閒營私沙礫雜和故色
愈變味愈惡而解鹽於是乎不可食矣民
日夕翹首以俟商之至而商之所貨乃如
此則其不樂售者豈情也哉於是商人坐
官肆終歲不能銷引目所在長吏又從而
代之斂散以取其值焉此不獨商困而民
亦困矣是以民視商若贅疣而視解之產
punctuated: 焉。夫解之有池，舊矣。歷代之張弛沿革，愚未暇悉也；昔所稱爲瑩潔如玉、卦美如穀，亦宇內之所共蝓也，愚不暇論也。祖宗時，額鹽僅十萬耳，至嘉靖中，始增至十九萬有奇。全晉、關、洛、梁、鄧之閒，皆其轉輸之所也。二百年來，公私俱足，在商人未嘗以山徑巉嶮稱難，在三省未嘗以解鹽苦惡爲病。何也？法一而志定也。自隆慶辛未，雨決池防，池水肆溢，鹽不結聚。當事者謂國計不可負，始爲澆曬之術，蓋以人力勝天時也。然而硝與鹽淆，不能一一而析之也。有姦商者出焉，乘閒營私，沙礫雜和，故色愈變、味愈惡，而解鹽於是乎不可食矣。民日夕翹首以俟商之至，而商之所貨乃如此，則其不樂售者，豈情也哉？於是商人坐官肆，終歲不能銷引目；所在長吏，又從而代之斂散以取其值焉。此不獨商困，而民亦困矣。是以民視商若贅疣，而視解之產
translation_en: … to the end. Now, the existence of the salt pond at Xie (Xiezhou 解州) is of long standing. I have no leisure to detail the expansions, relaxations, and institutional changes of past dynasties; nor do I have leisure to discuss how in former times it was praised as lustrous and pure as jade, or crystalline [?] and fine as grain—something known to all within the realm [?]. In the time of the Imperial Ancestors, the salt quota was only a hundred thousand yin; it was not until the Jiajing 嘉靖 reign (1522–1566) that it was increased to more than one hundred and ninety thousand. The entire region of Jin (Shanxi 山西), Guan (Shaanxi 陕西), Luo (Luoyang 洛陽), Liang (Kaifeng 開封), and Deng (Dengzhou 鄧州) was the area to which it was transported and distributed. For two hundred years, both public and private needs were fully met. On the part of the merchants, they never complained of the difficulty of the precipitous mountain paths; on the part of the three provinces, they never suffered from Xie salt being bitter or foul. Why was this? Because the laws were unified and expectations were settled. Since the xinwei year of the Longqing 隆慶 reign (1571), when rain breached the pond's dikes and the pond water overflowed wildly, the salt failed to crystallize and gather. Those in charge of affairs, holding that the state finances must not be failed, first instituted the method of pouring and sun-drying, seeking by human effort to overcome the seasons of Heaven. Yet glauber's salt (nitre) and table salt became mixed together and could not be separated one by one. Dishonest merchants then emerged, taking advantage of the opportunity to pursue private gain by mixing in sand and gravel. Consequently, its color changed further for the worse and its taste grew ever more foul, until Xie salt became inedible. The people craned their necks day and night waiting for the merchants to arrive, yet when the goods the merchants sold were like this, how could their reluctance to buy be anything but natural? Thereupon, the merchants sat in the official shops and throughout the entire year were unable to clear their salt licenses (yinmu 引目). The chief local officials in those places then stepped in to distribute the salt and collect the price on their behalf. By this, not only were the merchants distressed, but the people too were distressed. For this reason, the people came to regard the merchants as a useless excrescence, and to regard the product of Xie …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
為斉物無不利於食私販者民利於食私
販而販者適至是謂兩相求兩相求則事
密官卒緝捕惟賄是餍販者餌之是謂兩
相利兩相利則防踈如是而淮蘆花馬之
產紛紛四至勢惡得而禁之哉間嘗銷退
引矣皆僞目也鹽儈四市而得之者也亦
嘗獲私販矣皆貧負也法所謂易米度日
者也夫私販盛則商利薄商利薄則國賦
病此而不爲之計將何所取盈哉所謂計
===
者非必分地改額以滋聚訟也亦非必盡
易其舊而創爲之法也愚所謂在酌其宜
而變通之耳其一曰慎採取之時夫解鹽
池產也與浙淮齊閩殊而反穡事浙淮齊
閩鬻海法也其利在地不在天其祛弊之
法在有餘不在不足乃解池則異是矣穡
事憂旱而池利旱且利南風古所稱阜財
解慍者是已夫天能使之常旱且南風乎
恒雨則結者融恒北風則升者下此其時
punctuated:
為斉物，無不利於食私販者。民利於食私販，而販者適至，是謂兩相求；兩相求則事密。官卒緝捕，惟賄是餍，販者餌之，是謂兩相利；兩相利則防踈。如是，而淮、蘆、花馬之產紛紛四至，勢惡得而禁之哉？間嘗銷退引矣，皆僞目也，鹽儈四市而得之者也；亦嘗獲私販矣，皆貧負也，法所謂易米度日者也。夫私販盛則商利薄，商利薄則國賦病，此而不爲之計，將何所取盈哉？

所謂計者，非必分地改額以滋聚訟也，亦非必盡易其舊而創爲之法也，愚所謂在酌其宜而變通之耳。

其一曰：慎採取之時。夫解鹽，池產也，與浙、淮、齊、閩殊，而反穡事。浙、淮、齊、閩，鬻海法也，其利在地不在天，其祛弊之法在有餘不在不足。乃解池則異是矣。穡事憂旱，而池利旱，且利南風，古所稱「阜財解慍」者是已。夫天能使之常旱且南風乎？恒雨則結者融，恒北風則升者下，此其時
translation_en:
… as ruined goods [?], so there is no one who does not find it advantageous to consume contraband salt. When the people find it advantageous to consume contraband salt and the smugglers happen to arrive, this is what is called mutual demand; when there is mutual demand, their dealings are kept secret. The official soldiers who patrol for and arrest them are only satisfied by bribes, and the smugglers bait them with these; this is what is called mutual benefit, and when there is mutual benefit, defenses grow lax. Under such conditions, when the salt products of the Huai, Changlu, and Huama regions pour in from all directions, how could the situation possibly be prohibited? Occasionally, expired salt certificates have been turned in and canceled, but they are all counterfeit documents obtained by salt brokers buying them up on all sides. Occasionally, salt smugglers have also been captured, but they are all impoverished peddlers carrying loads on their backs—those whom the law describes as trading salt for rice to get through the day. Now, when smuggling flourishes, the merchants' profits are thin; when the merchants' profits are thin, the state's revenue suffers. If we do not devise a plan for this, from where shall we obtain a full quota?

What is meant by a plan does not necessarily mean dividing the distribution territories or altering the quotas, thereby multiplying contentious debates; nor does it necessarily mean completely changing the old ways and creating new laws. What I mean lies simply in weighing what is appropriate and flexibly adapting to it.

The first point is: be attentive to the timing of harvesting. Now, Xiezhou salt is the product of a salt lake; it differs from the salt of Zhejiang, Huai, Shandong (Qi), and Fujian (Min), and its requirements are the opposite of farming. In Zhejiang, Huai, Shandong, and Fujian, the method is to boil seawater; its advantage lies in the earth and not in heaven, and the method for eliminating abuses there deals with surplus rather than shortage. The Xiezhou salt lake, however, is different from this. Farming fears drought, whereas the salt lake benefits from drought, and moreover benefits from the south wind—this is indeed what the ancients referred to as "increasing wealth and dispelling resentment." Yet can Heaven cause there always to be drought and a south wind? When there is constant rain, what has crystallized melts away; when there is a constant north wind, what has risen to the surface sinks back down. Thus its timing…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
爲難鹽丁散處諸邑旣難遽集𢧐其集而
圖之則已解矣非預以待之不可也春夏
𠔃期此凝結之候也羣各丁而聚諸池𠔃
失其會暇則驅之採草以資蓋藏固未嘗
虛其力矣矧若輩皆正役豈故淹之哉是
採辦之所宜講也二曰廣召募之役池跨
解安邑地近百里矣勢甚遼闊鹽丁僅二
萬餘取奚遍採之不遍地之所以有遺利
也嘉靖丙午鹽嘗盛生矣募近民雜採之
===
官取其七而以三充賞其利厚也競趨之
已而與之一已而存其鹽而給以値又不
以時於是召之不應矣夫民之潰手足裂
肌膚而不憚者逐利也顧賞若是是督之
遠也愚以爲宜厚之也試令近地之民毋
論千萬置之長貳而籍其名於官則朝結
而夕可集也民之趨利猶水也利則孰不
則去往有定令矣而自食之是上不信也
今宜遠其報成而給以二仍朝驗而夕惠
punctuated: 爲難。鹽丁散處諸邑，旣難遽集，𢧐其集而圖之，則已解矣，非預以待之不可也。春夏𠔃期，此凝結之候也。羣各丁而聚諸池，𠔃失其會；暇則驅之採草，以資蓋藏，固未嘗虛其力矣。矧若輩皆正役，豈故淹之哉？是採辦之所宜講也。二曰廣召募之役。池跨解、安邑地近百里矣，勢甚遼闊，鹽丁僅二萬餘，取奚遍？採之不遍，地之所以有遺利也。嘉靖丙午，鹽嘗盛生矣，募近民雜採之，官取其七，而以三充賞，其利厚也，競趨之。已而與之一，已而存其鹽而給以値，又不以時，於是召之不應矣。夫民之潰手足、裂肌膚而不憚者，逐利也。顧賞若是，是督之遠也，愚以爲宜厚之也。試令近地之民，毋論千萬，置之長貳，而籍其名於官，則朝結而夕可集也。民之趨利猶水也，利則孰不則去？往有定令矣，而自食之，是上不信也。今宜遠其報成，而給以二，仍朝驗而夕惠…
translation_en:
…is difficult. The salt workers are scattered across the various districts and are already hard to assemble quickly; if one waits until they have assembled before planning to harvest it, the salt will have already melted. Thus, one cannot but wait in readiness beforehand. The juncture of spring and summer [?] is the season when the salt crystallizes. If we gather the various workers and assemble them at the pond, we will not [?] miss the opportune moment; in their spare time, we can set them to cutting grass to provide material for covering and storing the salt, so their labor is certainly never wasted. Moreover, since these men are all performing their regular corvée service, how could this be considered deliberately detaining them? This is what ought to be carefully considered regarding the harvesting operations.

Second, broaden the recruitment of hired laborers. The salt pond spans the territory of Xiezhou 解州 and Anyi 安邑 for nearly a hundred li. Its expanse is vast, yet the registered salt workers number only slightly over twenty thousand—how can they harvest it all? When harvesting does not reach everywhere, the land leaves behind uncollected profit. In the bingwu year of the Jiajing reign (1546), salt once formed in great abundance. Nearby commoners were recruited to harvest it alongside the regular workers; the government took seven-tenths and used three-tenths as their reward. Because the profit was generous, people vied to flock to it. Later, they were given only one-tenth; later still, the government retained all the salt and paid them its value in cash, and even that was not paid on time. Consequently, when summoned, they no longer responded. Now, the reason commoners do not shrink from blistered hands and feet or chapped skin is that they are pursuing profit. Yet if the reward is like this, it drives them away; I believe they ought to be treated generously. Suppose we allow the people of the nearby areas, whether by the thousands or ten thousands, to be organized under chiefs and deputies with their names registered with the authorities; then when the salt crystallizes in the morning, they can be assembled by evening. The people's rush toward profit is like flowing water: if there is profit, who would not [come; if not, who would not] [?] leave? In the past there was an established regulation, yet the authorities went back on their own word—this was a failure of trust on the part of superiors. Now we ought to follow [?] their reporting of completed harvests and grant them two-tenths, while inspecting the salt in the morning and bestowing the reward by evening…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
之毋令胥史持簿書而肆為呵索民其有
不樂於赴者哉赴益衆則採益時採益時
則入益富一歲而不獲數歲之利者不然
也此足以待凶年之額胡為較錙銖而遺
遠慮乎三曰貴採取之精夫各丁募夫羣
然並集不憂其入之不厚矣在官司或急
成料以希功在丁夫或急採取以充數寧
無雜硝石而並進者乎則分區畫地以程
其工驗料計直以定其等屏惡存美以待
===
夫商皆不可不為之慮也四曰別遠近之
地夫鹽鹽非惡也稍帶硝性試灼以火則
騰越而上無異池鹽此法河東諳之而遠
人未諳也今鹽亦無幾矣請以待近之求
而減其價以為耗遠征之商非池鹽不給
則轉輸者皆飴鹽而商無不售之值民無
境外之求矣五曰循支給之法夫所謂超
支者非旋中旋支以勸商者乎商人中納
次第掣支例也往以池鹽未結曬鹽未充
punctuated:
之，毋令胥史持簿書而肆為呵索，民其有不樂於赴者哉？赴益衆則採益時，採益時則入益富。一歲而不獲數歲之利者，不然也。此足以待凶年之額，胡為較錙銖而遺遠慮乎？

三曰貴採取之精。夫各丁、募夫羣然並集，不憂其入之不厚矣。在官司或急成料以希功，在丁夫或急採取以充數，寧無雜硝石而並進者乎？則分區畫地以程其工，驗料計直以定其等，屏惡存美以待夫商，皆不可不為之慮也。

四曰別遠近之地。夫鹽鹽非惡也，稍帶硝性。試灼以火，則騰越而上，無異池鹽。此法河東諳之，而遠人未諳也。今鹽亦無幾矣，請以待近之求，而減其價以為耗。遠征之商，非池鹽不給，則轉輸者皆飴鹽，而商無不售之值，民無境外之求矣。

五曰循支給之法。夫所謂超支者，非旋中旋支以勸商者乎？商人中納，次第掣支，例也。往以池鹽未結，曬鹽未充，
translation_en:
… them, and do not allow clerks to hold the registers and wantonly berate and extort from them; would the people then not gladly flock to the work? The more numerous those who come, the more timely the harvesting; the more timely the harvesting, the more abundant the yield. That a single year should fail to yield the profit of several years would not be the case. This would be sufficient to meet the quotas for years of dearth; why then haggle over trifles and neglect long-term planning?

Third is to value refinement in harvesting. When the registered salt-workers and hired laborers gather together in crowds, there is no worry that the intake will not be abundant. Yet if officials, eager to claim merit, rush the finished product, or if laborers, eager to fill their quotas, rush the harvesting, how could they avoid mixing in saltpeter and presenting them together? Therefore, dividing the zones and demarcating the ground to measure their work, inspecting the material and calculating its value to determine its grade, and discarding the inferior while preserving the fine to await the merchants—all of these are matters that must be carefully planned for.

Fourth is to distinguish between near and distant places. Now, [sun-dried] salt [? 鹽鹽, likely 曬鹽] is not bad, though it slightly carries the properties of saltpeter. If one tries heating it with fire, the saltpeter rises up and dissipates, making it no different from lake salt. The people of Hedong Hedong 河東 are familiar with this method, whereas people from afar are not. Moreover, there is not much of this salt now. I ask that it be reserved to meet nearby demand, with its price reduced to account for the wastage during refining. As for merchants traveling from afar, if they are issued nothing but lake salt, then what is transported will all be sweet salt (yiyan 飴鹽); the merchants will have no goods that fail to fetch their price, and the people will have no need to seek salt from beyond the borders.

Fifth is to follow the regulations for disbursement. Is not what is called "expedited disbursement" (chaozhi 超支) meant to encourage merchants by disbursing salt immediately upon their delivery of grain? That merchants deliver grain and draw their salt in sequence is the established rule. In the past, because the lake salt had not yet crystallized and the sun-dried salt was not yet sufficient, …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
無以給商而責之入乃隨募小販給以澆
曬而籍其貲萬不得已之計耳而商人之
停支者迄今遂不可復夫商傾貲以入公
家以恒產在池也乃視其生而不得支何
以異於農之耕耨而不得穫者哉今池平
而花漸結矣採以時則蓄且倍也請絕小
販之招以優舊商之困可乎六曰均商民
之惠夫商人經年守支
國課取足人情之所當優者也然而此輩則
===
無厭矣籍口曬鹽肆爲揷和以吞壟斷之
計是故所在居民弃官鹽而樂私販爲官
司者又從而强所不樂民之無告甚矣今
宜遍檄諸司凡諸商無樣鹽卽係飾僞樣
鹽非官記卽是私封沒其貲而置之法一
懲而百警矣則商安所售其術而民有不
樂於商之至者乎七曰禁太汾之票何者
二郡固全晉之半也地多斥鹵掾而煎之
轉相輸販已非正法頃從其便給販者以
punctuated:
無以給商，而責之入，乃隨募小販，給以澆曬，而籍其貲，萬不得已之計耳；而商人之停支者，迄今遂不可復。夫商傾貲以入公家，以恒產在池也，乃視其生而不得支，何以異於農之耕耨而不得穫者哉？今池平而花漸結矣，採以時則蓄且倍也。請絕小販之招，以優舊商之困，可乎？

六曰均商民之惠。夫商人經年守支，國課取足，人情之所當優者也。然而此輩則無厭矣，籍口曬鹽，肆爲揷和，以吞壟斷之計。是故所在居民，弃官鹽而樂私販，爲官司者又從而强所不樂，民之無告甚矣。今宜遍檄諸司，凡諸商無樣鹽卽係飾僞，樣鹽非官記卽是私封，沒其貲而置之法，一懲而百警矣。則商安所售其術，而民有不樂於商之至者乎？

七曰禁太、汾之票。何者？二郡固全晉之半也，地多斥鹵，掾而煎之，轉相輸販，已非正法。頃從其便，給販者以
translation_en:
…there was nothing with which to supply the merchants, yet they were still pressed for revenue. Thus peddlers were recruited on the spot, supplied with watered and sun-dried salt, and their funds registered—a measure taken only out of utter necessity. Yet for those regular merchants whose salt allotments were suspended, restoration has remained impossible to this day. Now, merchants exhaust their capital to contribute to the state because their permanent livelihood lies in the salt pond. To watch the salt form and yet be unable to draw their allotment—how does this differ from farmers who plow and weed yet are not allowed to harvest? Now the pond has stabilized and the salt crystals are gradually forming; if harvested in season, the reserves will double. May I request that we cease recruiting petty peddlers so as to relieve the hardship of the established merchants?

Sixth: equalize the benefits for both merchants and the common people. Merchants wait year after year to draw their salt allotments, and state fiscal quotas depend on them for fulfillment; by human sentiment, they ought to be treated generously. Yet these men are insatiable! Using sun-dried salt as an excuse, they unscrupulously adulterate the product in order to pursue monopolistic profits. Consequently, local residents everywhere abandon government salt and gladly buy from private smugglers, while the authorities in turn force upon the people what they dislike, leaving the populace with nowhere to appeal. We should now issue circulars to all offices: whenever a merchant has no sample salt, it is to be deemed fraudulent; and whenever the sample salt lacks an official seal, it is to be deemed privately sealed. Confiscate their goods and subject them to the law—punishing one will warn a hundred. Where then will merchants peddle their tricks, and how could the people not rejoice at the merchants' arrival?

Seventh: prohibit the salt tickets of Taiyuan and Fenzhou. Why? Those two prefectures actually make up half of all Shanxi. Their land is full of saline flats; scraping [?] the earth and boiling it, then transporting and peddling the salt to one another, is already contrary to the proper regulations. Recently, for convenience's sake, peddlers were issued…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
券而歲徵其入此小票之所由名也彼堵
自食其有矣解鹽入其境終歲東閣竟莫
能售夫二郡去河東纔數舍耳法已莫可
詰彼遠者奚讓焉矧二郡之民動以一田
兩稅爲口實正謂業已供邊儲而又以輸
鹽課且并其所謂私販者而忘之矣此非
當禁之一耶夫惟愼天時也廣召募也精
採辦也則盡人之力者盡地之利所謂生
之貴裕其源者此也惟辨遠近也循舊例
===
也均商民也革煎販也則商無滯貨者民
無艱食所謂救之貴通其變者此也此則
不必分地而流布者自廣不必改額而壅
滯者自行民亦何所爲而顧食私販以博
罪哉雖然此皆自池鹽已生者計之也萬
一事勢如昔當奈何嗚呼池之利在天不
在人前已陳之矣夫鹽盡公課也鹽務盡
公務也王者有分土無分民故以河東視
三省誠難撓越若自
punctuated:
券，而歲徵其入，此小票之所由名也。彼堵自食其有矣，解鹽入其境，終歲東閣，竟莫能售。夫二郡去河東纔數舍耳，法已莫可詰，彼遠者奚讓焉？矧二郡之民，動以「一田兩稅」爲口實，正謂業已供邊儲，而又以輸鹽課，且并其所謂私販者而忘之矣。此非當禁之一耶？

夫惟愼天時也，廣召募也，精採辦也，則盡人之力者盡地之利，所謂「生之貴裕其源」者，此也；惟辨遠近也，循舊例也，均商民也，革煎販也，則商無滯貨者民無艱食，所謂「救之貴通其變」者，此也。此則不必分地而流布者自廣，不必改額而壅滯者自行，民亦何所爲而顧食私販以博罪哉？

雖然，此皆自池鹽已生者計之也，萬一事勢如昔，當奈何？嗚呼！池之利在天不在人，前已陳之矣。夫鹽盡公課也，鹽務盡公務也，王者有分土無分民。故以河東視三省，誠難撓越；若自
translation_en:
… certificates, and collecting the revenue from them annually—this is how the "small tickets" (xiaopiao) got their name. When those localities [?] all consume their own local supply, the salt from Xiezhou that enters their territory is shelved away the entire year and ultimately cannot be sold. Now, those two prefectures [Taiyuan and Fenzhou] are only a few stages away from Hedong, yet the law already cannot be enforced there; why then should more distant places yield to it? Moreover, the people of these two prefectures constantly use "one field paying two taxes" as a pretext—meaning that they already supply the frontier reserves and on top of that must pay the salt tax—and in doing so they have completely forgotten that what they are engaging in is illicit trafficking! Is this not one of the things that ought to be prohibited?

Now, only by heeding the seasons of Heaven, expanding recruitment, and refining the process of harvesting and procurement will the full exertion of human effort exhaust the advantages of the earth; this is what was meant by "in producing it, the key is to enrich its source." And only by distinguishing between near and far, following the old precedents, balancing the interests of merchants and the people, and abolishing boiled-earth salt trafficking will merchants have no stagnant goods and the people suffer no scarcity of salt for food; this is what was meant by "in remedying it, the key is to adapt to changing circumstances." In this way, without needing to repartition the distribution territories, circulation will naturally widen; without needing to alter the quotas, what was clogged will naturally flow. For what reason, then, would the people still consume contraband salt just to court punishment?

Even so, all of these calculations assume that the pond salt has already crystallized. If by some chance the situation returns to what it was before, what should be done? Alas! That the bounty of the salt pond depends on Heaven and not on man has already been set forth above. Yet all salt revenue is public tax, and all salt administration is public business; a true king divides the land into jurisdictions, but does not divide the people. Therefore, if one views the three provinces from the perspective of Hedong, it is indeed difficult to cross jurisdictional bounds; but if from the perspective of…

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
國家統觀之則安可執一論也拓存積之淮
蘆充有餘之花馬以寬不足之河東蘘其
生結而各還其舊奚不可者夫據時宜而
談利害環池之人類能言之至問上不病
國中不病民下不病法則鉅公大人謇謇
不欲語者何者狃於法之故也愚生之見
若是孰事其財擇焉
第五問
何東鳳
===
同考試官教諭梁　批〔立邊設防建官責守我〕
國家之制原自周詳惟在當事者實心幹濟耳誠無庸紛更爲也此作發出可爲邊臣忠告
考試官學正梅　批〔三關責守事體論議明當〕
考試官教授朱　批〔通達邊務〕
善守邊者不拘於地善籌邊者不拘於守
夫今議邊事者守爲上策矣而曩者虜蹂
踐我內地材官騎士環視不能當一戰固
戰不如守之明效也矧今天實不逞於虜
畏威悔禍而吾得備之暇哉此議守之時
punctuated:
國家統觀之，則安可執一論也？拓存積之淮、蘆，充有餘之花馬，以寬不足之河東，蘘其生結而各還其舊，奚不可者？夫據時宜而談利害，環池之人類能言之；至問上不病國，中不病民，下不病法，則鉅公大人謇謇不欲語者，何者？狃於法之故也。愚生之見若是，孰事其財擇焉。

第五問
何東鳳
同考試官教諭梁　批：〔立邊設防，建官責守，我〕國家之制原自周詳，惟在當事者實心幹濟耳，誠無庸紛更爲也。此作發出，可爲邊臣忠告。
考試官學正梅　批：〔三關責守事體，論議明當。〕
考試官教授朱　批：〔通達邊務。〕

善守邊者不拘於地，善籌邊者不拘於守。夫今議邊事者，守爲上策矣。而曩者虜蹂踐我內地，材官騎士環視不能當一戰，固戰不如守之明效也；矧今天實不逞於虜，畏威悔禍，而吾得備之暇哉！此議守之時
translation_en:
… viewed comprehensively from the perspective of the dynasty as a whole, how can one cling to a single rigid argument? Expanding the stockpiled salt of Huai and Changlu, and drawing upon the surplus of the Huama Salt Pond in order to relieve the shortfall in Hedong—hoping [蘘 for 冀?] that the salt will form and crystallize so that each region may then return to its former arrangement—why should this be impossible? Now, as for discussing advantages and disadvantages on the basis of timely expediency, the people living around the salt pond can mostly speak of such things; yet when asked how to avoid harming the state above, harming the people in the middle, and harming the laws below, even great officials and eminent men hesitate and are unwilling to speak. Why is this? Because they are bound by habit to the existing laws. Such are the views of this humble student; may those in charge of affairs [孰事 for 執事?] judge and select from them [財擇 for 裁擇].

Fifth Question
He Dongfeng 何東鳳
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Liang comments: [Establishing frontiers and setting up defenses, appointing officials and assigning responsibilities for guarding—the] institutions of our dynasty have always been thorough and detailed; everything depends solely on those in charge carrying them out with genuine commitment, and there is truly no need for tumultuous changes. What this essay sets forth can serve as loyal counsel for frontier officials.
Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Mei comments: [On the system of responsibilities for defending the Three Passes, the discussion and arguments are clear and fitting.]
Examiner and Prefectural Director of Studies Zhu comments: [Thoroughly conversant with frontier affairs.]

Those skilled at defending the frontier are not bound by territory; those skilled at planning for the frontier are not bound merely to defense. Now, among those who deliberate on frontier affairs today, defense is regarded as the supreme strategy. In the past, when the caitiffs trampled our interior lands, our skilled soldiers and cavalrymen looked on from all sides without being able to withstand a single battle—this was certainly clear proof that fighting is inferior to defending. How much more so today, when Heaven truly denies success to the caitiffs, so that they stand in awe of our might and repent of the calamities they caused, affording us the leisure to make preparations! This is the time to deliberate on defense …

title: 萬曆四年山西鄉試錄
text:
也雖然未易輕議也其本在人其要在勢
山西右屛
畿輔外鄰沙漠所稱爲幷冀藩垣者北則大
同大同之南褁寧鴈而折而之西則有偏
老大同之邊虜也近不一舍遠不二三舍
偏老亦然夫大同後固有專之者矣如偏
老寧鴈所謂三關也三關之形若鱗次然
東稍南爲鴈門百八十里抵寧武又二百
里抵偏關偏關絕懸西北與大同峙而鴈
===
門寧武者則猶有馬邑朔州之爲外藩也
往以大同不能爲蔽故議與晝地而守之
三關節制以屬全晉之撫臣而移總戎之
駐偏頭者駐寧武若爲居中調度備東西
策應也近籌邊者更議以爲不便謂弃外
郋內或以外地委敵而撫臣距疆埸旣遠
藉於請質之難偏裨孤居卒不得籍援於
大將欲以撫鎭槩置偏老與大同相犄角
幷力要害脫虜自馬邑朔州入犯而吾犄
punctuated: 也。雖然，未易輕議也。其本在人，其要在勢。山西右屛畿輔，外鄰沙漠，所稱爲幷、冀藩垣者，北則大同，大同之南褁寧、鴈，而折而之西則有偏、老。大同之邊虜也，近不一舍，遠不二三舍，偏、老亦然。夫大同後固有專之者矣，如偏、老、寧、鴈，所謂三關也。三關之形若鱗次然，東稍南爲鴈門，百八十里抵寧武，又二百里抵偏關。偏關絕懸西北，與大同峙，而鴈門、寧武者，則猶有馬邑、朔州之爲外藩也。往以大同不能爲蔽，故議與晝地而守之，三關節制以屬全晉之撫臣，而移總戎之駐偏頭者駐寧武，若爲居中調度、備東西策應也。近籌邊者更議以爲不便，謂弃外郋內，或以外地委敵；而撫臣距疆埸旣遠，藉於請質之難；偏裨孤居，卒不得籍援於大將。欲以撫、鎭槩置偏、老，與大同相犄角，幷力要害；脫虜自馬邑、朔州入犯，而吾犄
translation_en:
… Yet even so, it is not a matter to be discussed lightly. Its foundation lies in men, and its crux lies in strategic configuration.

Shanxi serves as the right-hand screen protecting the Metropolitan Area and borders the desert wastes on the outside.
